title: Gradient-boosted trees are the default for tabular data
content: On medium-sized tabular datasets, gradient-boosted decision trees (HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM) usually outperform deep networks and linear models. HistGradientBoosting handles missing values natively and scales to 100k+ rows. Tune learning_rate (0.03-0.1), max_iter (200-1000) and max_leaf_nodes (15-63).

title: Random forests are robust low-tuning baselines
content: Random forests and extra-trees need little tuning, resist overfitting on small data, and give feature importances. 300-500 trees with max_features='sqrt' (classification) is a strong default. They are slower than histogram boosting on large data.

title: Linear models need scaling and encoding
content: Logistic regression, ridge and lasso are fast, interpretable baselines. They require standardized numeric features and one-hot encoded categoricals, and benefit from regularization tuning (C or alpha on a log grid). Good when n_samples is small relative to n_features.

title: Handling class imbalance
content: With imbalanced labels, prefer f1_macro, balanced_accuracy or roc_auc over accuracy. Use stratified splits and class_weight='balanced' (logistic regression, SVM, random forest) instead of naive oversampling.

title: Missing values and categorical encoding
content: Impute numeric columns with the median and categoricals with the most frequent value (or a 'missing' category). One-hot encode low-cardinality categoricals; cap or group rare levels for high-cardinality ones. Drop identifier columns: they leak nothing useful and cause overfitting.

title: SVM and kNN scale poorly
content: RBF-kernel SVMs and k-nearest neighbours can do well on small (<10k rows), well-scaled numeric data but become slow and memory-hungry on larger datasets. Always standardize features first.

title: Regression targets and metrics
content: For skewed positive targets (prices, counts) consider a log transform of the target. RMSE penalizes large errors, MAE is robust to outliers, R2 is scale-free. Report more than one.

title: TF-IDF + linear models are strong text baselines
content: For text classification with limited compute, TF-IDF over word 1-2 grams (sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2) followed by a linear SVM or logistic regression is fast and competitive. Complement Naive Bayes works well on short texts and small data. SGD scales to very large corpora.

title: Fine-tuned transformers for higher accuracy
content: When a GPU is available and the dataset has thousands of labeled examples, fine-tuning a small pretrained transformer (DistilBERT, MiniLM) typically beats TF-IDF baselines by several points. On CPU-only setups prefer TF-IDF models.

title: Validation strategy
content: Use a stratified 80/20 hold-out for quick evaluation and 5-fold cross-validation when data is small (<2k rows). Fix random seeds for reproducibility and never fit preprocessing on the test split (wrap everything in a Pipeline).

title: Time-series forecasting with LightGBM and statistical baselines
content: For time-series forecasting, always compare machine learning models against statistical baselines like Seasonal Naive and Exponential Smoothing (ETS), which act as performance floors. A global LightGBM model trained across all series using lag features, rolling statistics (mean, std), and calendar features (day of week, month) forms a strong baseline. Use direct multi-horizon forecasting to avoid recursive error accumulation, and evaluate using sMAPE, MAE, or RMSE.

title: Temporal splits and leakage prevention for time series
content: Time-series data must always be partitioned using contiguous temporal splits (train -> validation -> test) without shuffling. Lag features and rolling statistics must be built strictly from the past relative to the forecast origin to prevent look-ahead target leakage. For successive-halving grounded verification, use suffix windows (most recent data) so low-fidelity rungs remain representative.
